case_info.scenario: A 62-year-old Japanese man was diagnosed with submandibular salivary duct carcinoma (T4bN3cM0 according to Union for International Cancer Control, 8th edition). He underwent right neck dissection with skin resection, reconstruction using a pectoralis major flap, and adjuvant radiotherapy (66 Gy). He remained free of recurrence on regular clinical and computed tomography (CT) surveillance but continued daily heavy alcohol consumption. Three years later, he developed progressive frailty with 3 months of reduced oral intake. Neurologic examination revealed diminished superficial sensation, dysesthesia, and impaired proprioception in the lower extremities, consistent with sensory ataxia in a polyneuropathy pattern. Laboratory testing at that time showed macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin, 9.1 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]; mean corpuscular volume, 101.4 μm3(to convert to femtoliters, multiply by 1), and vitamin B12supplementation was initiated. Spinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), performed to evaluate for structural causes of neurologic symptoms, revealed multiple hypointense lesions on T1-weighted images in the thoracolumbar spine (Figure 1A); similar findings were observed on T2-weighted imaging (image not shown). The corresponding CT image demonstrated mild hyperdensity with ill-defined margins without cortical destruction (Figure 1B). Given his oncologic history and the imaging findings, a CT-guided biopsy of the signal alteration in the T12 vertebral body was performed by an orthopedic spine surgeon for definitive diagnosis.

case_info.explanation: Histological examination revealed trabecular bone without epithelial elements, and immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin (AE1/AE3) was negative. The bone marrow demonstrated normal trilineage hematopoiesis, with no evidence of malignancy. Although positron emission tomography (PET)/CT was not performed at that time, a retrospective review of a PET/CT scan obtained 3 years earlier revealed mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the thoracolumbar vertebral bodies (Figure 2). In the context of the patient’s clinical and imaging findings, these results are supportive of bone pseudometastasis.1This phenomenon has been predominantly reported in East Asian patients with esophageal cancer and, less frequently, in head and neck cancers.2,3 While biopsy remains the criterion standard for establishing the diagnosis, several imaging features can suggest bone pseudometastasis. Typical imaging shows hypointense lesions on T1/T2 MRI and mild hyperdensity without cortical destruction on CT.1Although these findings are nonspecific, the absence of aggressive features such as cortical destruction or soft tissue extension may help raise suspicion for a benign process. Serial imaging is also informative, as pseudometastatic lesions typically remain stable over time. In general, PET-CT may show mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake with lower standardized uptake values but cannot reliably distinguish pseudometastasis from true metastasis.1,3 The pathophysiology of bone pseudometastasis remains incompletely understood. Proposed mechanisms include alterations of the marrow microenvironment associated with chronic alcohol consumption and ALDH2 deficiency, which may influence hematopoietic activity, a hypothesis supported by frequent reports in Japanese patients with esophageal cancer, where ALDH2 deficiency is a known risk factor. Reported cases frequently demonstrated anemia or subsequent hematologic disorders such as myelodysplastic syndrome, suggesting that impaired or heterogeneous hematopoiesis and red marrow reconversion play central roles in its development.3Other plausible causes—malnutrition, prior irradiation, or intraosseous venous malformations—were unlikely: no irradiation history, no imaging evidence, and stability despite nutritional correction. Prior reports also showed benign hematopoietic marrow without tumor infiltration, consistent with the present case.1,2 Answer A was incorrect. In salivary duct carcinoma, approximately 15% develop bone metastases that can be lytic/sclerotic/mixed and mimic benignity; tissue diagnosis is essential.4Answer B was also incorrect.  Prostate metastases are typically osteoblastic with T1 low and T2 iso-low signal plus restricted diffusion, usually in older men with high prostate-specific antigen, which was absent here.5Answer C was incorrect as well. Myelofibrosis causes diffuse, symmetric low T1/T2 spinal signal, unlike this focal pattern.6 Recognizing these imaging patterns in context can avert unnecessary interventions and misdiagnosis; integrate clinicoradiologic correlation; and, when needed, pathologic confirmation or interval imaging to avoid missing true bone metastases.

case_info.explanation: Histological examination revealed trabecular bone without epithelial elements, and immunohistochemical staining for cytokeratin (AE1/AE3) was negative. Although positron emission tomography (PET)/CT was not performed at that time, a retrospective review of a PET/CT scan obtained 3 years earlier revealed mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the thoracolumbar vertebral bodies (Figure 2). In the context of the patient’s clinical and imaging findings, these results are supportive of bone pseudometastasis.1This phenomenon has been predominantly reported in East Asian patients with esophageal cancer and, less frequently, in head and neck cancers.2,3 While biopsy remains the criterion standard for establishing the diagnosis, several imaging features can suggest bone pseudometastasis. Typical imaging shows hypointense lesions on T1/T2 MRI and mild hyperdensity without cortical destruction on CT.1Although these findings are nonspecific, the absence of aggressive features such as cortical destruction or soft tissue extension may help raise suspicion for a benign process. Serial imaging is also informative, as pseudometastatic lesions typically remain stable over time. In general, PET-CT may show mild fluorodeoxyglucose uptake with lower standardized uptake values but cannot reliably distinguish pseudometastasis from true metastasis.1,3 The pathophysiology of bone pseudometastasis remains incompletely understood. Proposed mechanisms include alterations of the marrow microenvironment associated with chronic alcohol consumption and ALDH2 deficiency, which may influence hematopoietic activity, a hypothesis supported by frequent reports in Japanese patients with esophageal cancer, where ALDH2 deficiency is a known risk factor. Reported cases frequently demonstrated anemia or subsequent hematologic disorders such as myelodysplastic syndrome, suggesting that impaired or heterogeneous hematopoiesis and red marrow reconversion play central roles in its development.3Other plausible causes—malnutrition, prior irradiation, or intraosseous venous malformations—were unlikely: no irradiation history, no imaging evidence, and stability despite nutritional correction. He underwent right neck dissection with skin resection, reconstruction using a pectoralis major flap, and adjuvant radiotherapy (66 Gy). He remained free of recurrence on regular clinical and computed tomography (CT) surveillance but continued daily heavy alcohol consumption. Three years later, he developed progressive frailty with 3 months of reduced oral intake. Neurologic examination revealed diminished superficial sensation, dysesthesia, and impaired proprioception in the lower extremities, consistent with sensory ataxia in a polyneuropathy pattern. Laboratory testing at that time showed macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin, 9.1 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]; mean corpuscular volume, 101.4 μm3(to convert to femtoliters, multiply by 1), and vitamin B12supplementation was initiated. Spinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), performed to evaluate for structural causes of neurologic symptoms, revealed multiple hypointense lesions on T1-weighted images in the thoracolumbar spine (Figure 1A); similar findings were observed on T2-weighted imaging (image not shown). The corresponding CT image demonstrated mild hyperdensity with ill-defined margins without cortical destruction (Figure 1B). Given his oncologic history and the imaging findings, a CT-guided biopsy of the signal alteration in the T12 vertebral body was performed by an orthopedic spine surgeon for definitive diagnosis.
